value: The retention intervals used in nonverbal auditory working-memory experiments, and whether they are long enough to exclude auditory sensory memory.
When a study reports working memory for a nonverbal sound after a few seconds, is it measuring working memory at all, or the sensory trace that persists alongside it?
Shows that the conventional 3-5 s retention interval does not exclude auditory sensory memory, so a body of findings attributed to working memory is ambiguous between two constructs.

quote: This assumption is examined in detail in this comment.

Unlike verbal working memory studies that use serial recall tasks, research paradigms for exploring nonverbal working memory—especially two-stimulus comparison tasks—may not be differentiating working memory from sensory memory processes in analyses of behavioral responses, because retention interval durations have not excluded the possibility that the sensory memory trace drives task performance.
Researchers have shown increased interest in mechanisms of working memory for nonverbal sounds such as music and environmental sounds.

value: auditory cognition; a commentary arguing that a methodological convention in nonverbal auditory working-memory research conflates two constructs

quote: Though some researchers have estimated it to be 2 s or less ( Crowder, 1976 ; Huron and Parncutt, 1993 ), longer estimates have included 3.5 s ( Mcevoy et al., 1997 ), 4–5 s ( Glucksberg and Cowen, 1970 ), at least several seconds ( Cowan, 1984 ), 10 s ( Sams et al., 1993 ), 10–15 s ( Winkler and Cowan, 2005 ), 20 s ( Watkins and Todres, 1980 ), at least 30 s ( Winkler et al., 2002 ), and possibly up to 60 s ( Engle and Roberts, 1982 ).

value: Retention intervals under 5 s fall inside most published estimates of sensory-memory persistence, while intervals of 8-10 s or more begin to exceed most of them.

value: No single safe retention interval can be recommended, because the duration of the sensory trace itself differs considerably from person to person.
quote: To complicate the matter further, evidence has suggested that the duration of ASM is subject to considerable individual differences (e.g., Kubovy and Howard, 1976 ).

value: Verbal serial recall separates the two stores by serial position - primacy indexes rehearsal in working memory and auditory recency indexes sensory memory - a dissociation that nonverbal comparison tasks cannot deliver.

value: Four incompatible mechanisms are currently proposed for working memory of nonverbal sounds: the verbal phonological loop, a separate music memory loop, attention, and different mechanisms for pitch versus timbre.
